To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) lipid biomarker analysis and compound specific δ 13C analysis of burned sand and organic residue from archaeological sites in northern Alaska indicates hunters were exploiting marine animal resources as far back as 4,500 years ago, and (2) the use of marine animals by the Arctic Small Tool Tradition is an important component of the early prehistoric economy in northern Alaska.
lipid analyses of organic residue features from five sites in northern Alaska indicate that ASTt hunters exploited marine animals, as early as 4,500 years ago.

the earliest Arctic Small Tools tradition (ASTt, 4500–3000 cal BP) hunters in northwest Alaska made use of marine animal resources, and lipid analysis can be a powerful tool for reconstructing early Arctic subsistence strategies.

the development of a dual-economy in the Arctic Small Tool Tradition.

the early history of the Arctic Small Tool Tradition (ASTT), a prehistoric culture in northwest Alaska that is generally considered to have developed in the interior of Alaska and then moved north and west into the Arctic coastal zone.
understanding the early development of an economic system in the Arctic Small Tool Tradition of northern Alaska, and the role marine resources played in this process.

the early Arctic Small Tool Tradition people in northwest Alaska were exploiting both marine and terrestrial animal resources.
